session.question: How are the SDOs linked to policy coherance for sustainable development in the EU context?
session.answer:
The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are used as a framework for assessing policy coherence for sustainable development in the EU because they span environmental, social, and economic dimensions and make trade-offs across policy domains visible. In this context, policy coherence refers to the extent to which policies are mutually supportive rather than contradictory, especially across sectors and governance levels. (coscieme2021enhanceenvironmentalpolicy chunk 1, gao2024theeu’stwin chunk 1)

Within the EU analysis, environmental goals were found to be the most complex and least coherent among the SDGs, indicating that coherence problems are most acute where environmental, biodiversity, and climate objectives intersect with other policy areas. This suggests that the SDGs function not only as targets but also as a diagnostic tool for identifying incoherence in EU sustainability governance. (coscieme2021enhanceenvironmentalpolicy chunk 1)

The literature also indicates that policy coherence has been central to the 2030 Agenda’s promise of “leaving no one behind,” but coherent policymaking does not automatically produce equitable outcomes. In the EU context, this reinforces the idea that coherence must be evaluated both for alignment among goals and for distributive effects, particularly when inequality is considered. (browne2023howdoespolicy chunk 1)

Accordingly, improving data availability and strengthening monitoring—especially for biodiversity- and climate-related SDGs—are presented as necessary conditions for enhancing policy coherence and informing financing and post-2030 agenda design. (coscieme2021enhanceenvironmentalpolicy chunk 1)

session.context:
pqac-28a421f0: The excerpt says that the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) provide a framework for tracking progress across environmental, social, and economic dimensions of sustainability, and that ensuring policy coherence among these goals is a major challenge. In the EU analysis, the authors found that environmental goals are the most complex and least coherent of all SDGs. They argue that improving data availability and strengthening monitoring, especially for biodiversity and climate-related SDGs, is necessary to enhance policy coherence and support sustainable development. The findings are meant to inform financing and post-2030 agenda design.
From Luca Coscieme, Lars Fogh Mortensen, and Ian Donohue. Enhance environmental policy coherence to meet the sustainable development goals. Journal of Cleaner Production, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2021.126502, doi:10.1016/j.jclepro.2021.126502.

pqac-44bc80ef: The excerpt describes a 2023 study on policy coherence and the SDGs, especially SDG 10 on inequality. It argues that policy coherence was promoted during the 2030 Agenda as a way to make policies more effective and ensure sustainable development that “leaves no one behind.” The review of 40 studies found that coherent policymaking did not reduce inequality in most cases and sometimes worsened it. However, the excerpt does not mention SDOs specifically or explain their link to policy coherence in the EU context.
From Katherine E. Browne, Adis Dzebo, Gabriela Iacobuţă, Alexia Faus Onbargi, Zoha Shawoo, Ines Dombrowsky, Mathias Fridahl, Sara Gottenhuber, and Åsa Persson. How does policy coherence shape effectiveness and inequality? implications for sustainable development and the 2030 agenda. Sustainable Development, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sd.2598, doi:10.1002/sd.2598.

pqac-758341e9: The excerpt is about the EU’s green and digital “twin transitions,” not SDOs specifically. It defines coherence as reducing contradictions across policy domains and assesses it along conceptual and operational dimensions, horizontally and vertically across governance levels. The study finds that alignment between policy areas and coordination across levels is widely recognized, but conceptual coherence differs by governance level and policy area, and operational coherence lags behind conceptual coherence. This framework could be relevant to policy coherence for sustainable development, but the excerpt does not mention SDOs or directly explain their link to policy coherence in the EU context.
From Xinchuchu Gao. The eu’s twin transitions towards sustainability and digital leadership: a coherent or fragmented policy field? Regional Studies, 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1080/00343404.2024.2360053, doi:10.1080/00343404.2024.2360053.

pqac-19708677: The excerpt does not mention SDOs (likely Sustainable Development Objectives/Goals) in detail or explain their linkage to policy coherence in the EU context. It only states that literature on policy coherence has grown especially since the diffusion of the 2030 Agenda, to understand intersectoral policymaking and governance complexity in sustainable development, environmental, and climate policies. The article finds that policy coherence has been studied mainly in relation to sustainable development, environment, climate change, and transboundary governance, with emphasis on the implementation phase. It also suggests future work should address neglected policy-process dimensions in a process-oriented framework.
From Maria Stella Righettini and Renata Lizzi. How scholars break down “policy coherence”: the impact of sustainable development global agendas on academic literature. Environmental Policy and Governance, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/eet.1966, doi:10.1002/eet.1966.

pqac-0a10562f: The excerpt does not mention SDOs or the EU context directly. It explains that the paper offers an analytical framework for policy coherence for sustainable development based on three political drivers—ideas, institutions, and interests (“the three I’s”). The framework focuses on how these drivers shape policy coherence at different stages, how different actors and institutions apply coherence, and whose ideas and interests are advanced or resisted. It is illustrated using coherence between Agenda 2030 and the Paris Agreement, and can be applied at global or national levels.
From Zoha Shawoo, Aaron Maltais, Adis Dzebo, and Jonathan Pickering. Political drivers of policy coherence for sustainable development: an analytical framework. Environmental Policy and Governance, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/eet.2039, doi:10.1002/eet.2039.
